subject: Surgery
topic: Surgical Wound Dehiscence Without Evisceration
stem:
A 64-year-old man who underwent an open exploratory laparotomy and Hartmann procedure for perforated diverticulitis 5 days ago is recovering on the surgical floor. He has a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 36 kg/m2), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. While coughing vigorously this morning, he felt a sudden 'pop' and tearing sensation along his midline abdominal incision, followed by a sudden gush of clear, pink, salmon-colored serosanguinous fluid soaking through his abdominal dressings. The surgical resident removes the dressing to inspect the incision. The superficial skin and subcutaneous adipose tissue have separated along an 8-cm segment of the midline incision. On careful sterile digital examination using sterile gloves, the deep rectus aponeurotic fascia is found to be intact, with no bowel loops, omentum, or peritoneal contents visible or protruding through the defect (absence of evisceration). Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 132/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 84/min, and temperature of 37.4 C. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen with mild expected perilesional tenderness and no peritoneal signs.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial management for this patient's wound complication?

options.text: Apply sterile, moist saline-soaked gauze dressings to the wound, support the abdomen with an abdominal binder, advise the patient to avoid strenuous coughing or Valsalva maneuvers, and arrange for secondary healing or delayed primary closure, withholding emergency laparotomy
options.explanation: Postoperative Wound Dehiscence is the separation of the margins of a surgical wound, occurring in 1% to 3% of abdominal surgeries: (1) RISK FACTORS: Malnutrition, obesity, advanced age, diabetes mellitus, systemic corticosteroids, intra-abdominal hypertension (vigorous coughing, retching, COPD, ileus), and surgical site infection. (2) PATHOGNOMONIC SIGN: The sudden, copious leakage of SALMON-COLORED (SEROSANGUINOUS) FLUID from an abdominal wound on postoperative days 4 to 8 is the classic hallmark of wound breakdown. (3) CRUCIAL TRIAGE - EVISCERATION VERSUS DEHISCENCE WITHOUT EVISCERATION: (a) WOUND EVISCERATION: Rupture of BOTH the fascial closure and the peritoneum, with protrusion of intra-abdominal viscera (bowel loops, omentum) out through the skin incision. Evisceration is an ABSOLUTE SURGICAL EMERGENCY requiring immediate covering with sterile moist saline sponges and emergent return to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy and fascial reconstruction. (b) DEHISCENCE WITHOUT EVISCERATION (SUPERFICIAL DEHISCENCE): In this patient, careful sterile examination confirms that the DEEP FASCIA IS INTACT, and no intra-abdominal contents protrude. Emergency laparotomy is NOT INDICATED. (4) MANAGEMENT OF SUPERFICIAL DEHISCENCE: (a) Local wound care with sterile moist saline dressings (or negative-pressure wound therapy [wound VAC]) to promote granulation tissue; (b) Application of an elastic abdominal binder to splint the incision and reduce tension; (c) Cough suppression and stool softeners to prevent spikes in intra-abdominal pressure; and (d) Healing by secondary intention or delayed secondary surgical closure once clean granulation tissue is established. (5) BEDSIDE SUTURING CONTRAINDICATION: Blindly placing deep sutures into an open, separated wound at the bedside is dangerous because it risks puncturing unseen underlying bowel and introduces foreign material into a contaminated wound.

options.text: Immediately return the patient to the operating room for emergent exploratory laparotomy and mesh placement
options.explanation: Emergent re-operation is indicated exclusively for complete fascial rupture with visceral evisceration; in superficial dehiscence with an intact deep fascia, emergency surgery is unnecessary and overly invasive.

options.text: Blindly re-approximate the separated wound margins at the bedside using 1-0 polypropylene interrupted retention sutures without local anesthesia
options.explanation: Blind bedside deep suturing risks catastrophic bowel perforation and fistula formation, causes severe pain, and traps bacteria within contaminated subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Pack the open wound with dry sterile gauze sponges and apply a rigid adhesive pressure dressing changed once weekly
options.explanation: Dry gauze desiccates exposed tissues, causes mechanical damage during removal, and weekly dressing changes promote bacterial infection; moist saline dressings changed regularly are required.

options.text: Administer intravenous vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and metronidazole for 14 days for presumed intra-abdominal sepsis
options.explanation: Superficial mechanical dehiscence without fever, erythema, purulence, or peritoneal signs is a mechanical complication, not a systemic bacterial infection; systemic antibiotics are not indicated.

topic: Post-Dural Puncture Headache (PDPH) and Epidural Blood Patch
stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida woman who underwent an uncomplicated elective repeat Cesarean delivery under epidural anesthesia 48 hours ago is recovering on the postpartum ward. During epidural catheter placement by a trainee, an accidental dural puncture ('wet tap') occurred with an 18-gauge Tuohy needle, but the catheter was resited successfully. This morning upon attempting to sit up in bed to nurse her newborn, she developed an excruciating, incapacitating, throbbing bifrontal and occipital headache radiating to her neck and shoulders. She describes that the headache is completely agonizing (10/10) when sitting or standing, but completely disappears within 5 to 10 minutes whenever she lies completely flat in the supine position. She also reports mild photophobia, nausea, and muffled hearing (tinnitus). Physical examination demonstrates an uncomfortable woman lying flat in bed. Vital signs are normal, and she is afebrile. Neurological examination is completely normal: pupils are reactive, cranial nerves are intact, motor and sensory exams are normal, and there is no papilledema or nuchal rigidity when supine. Conservative management with aggressive oral and intravenous hydration, oral acetaminophen, oral caffeine, and bed rest was initiated 24 hours ago, but her headache recurs with unbearable intensity whenever she attempts to stand.

Which of the following represents the most effective definitive therapeutic intervention for this patient's condition?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days to suppress meningeal inflammation
options.explanation: PDPH is a mechanical CSF leak causing downward brain traction, not an autoimmune or inflammatory condition; corticosteroids provide zero therapeutic benefit and delay definitive mechanical repair.

options.text: Perform an autologous epidural blood patch (injecting 15 to 20 mL of the patient's own sterile venous blood into the epidural space at or near the level of the dural puncture)
options.explanation: Post-Dural Puncture Headache (PDPH) is a classic iatrogenic complication resulting from intentional or accidental perforation of the dura mater during spinal anesthesia, diagnostic lumbar puncture, or epidural placement: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Cerebrospinal fluid leaks continuously through the persistent dural-arachnoid puncture hole into the epidural space at a rate faster than choroid plexus CSF production (normal CSF production is ~0.35 mL/min or 500 mL/day). This causes intracranial CSF hypovolemia and low intracranial pressure. When the patient assumes an upright posture, the brain sags downward within the cranial vault, placing traction on pain-sensitive anchoring structures (the tentorium cerebelli, dural falx, and sensory branches of cranial nerves V, IX, X). Compensatory cerebral and meningeal venodilation also contributes to throbbing pain. (2) PATHOGNOMONIC CLINICAL HALLMARK: An intensely POSTURAL / ORTHOSTATIC HEADACHE that worsens significantly within 15 minutes of sitting or standing and resolves or improves markedly within 15 to 30 minutes of lying supine. Auditory symptoms (tinnitus, hearing loss) occur due to endolymphatic sac pressure changes. (3) DEFINITIVE THERAPY (THE AUTOLOGOUS EPIDURAL BLOOD PATCH): While mild PDPH can be managed conservatively for 24 to 48 hours (bed rest, hydration, caffeine, NSAIDs), an AUTOLOGOUS EPIDURAL BLOOD PATCH (EBP) is the DEFINITIVE GOLD STANDARD OF CARE for severe, incapacitating PDPH or cases refractory to conservative therapy. Protocol: Under strict aseptic technique, 15 to 20 mL of the patient's own autologous blood is drawn from an antecubital vein and injected into the epidural space at or adjacent to the level of the dural puncture. The blood spreads several spinal segments cephalad and caudad, forming a gelatinous fibrin clot that mechanically plugs the dural tear, immediately halting further CSF leak and restoring normal intracranial CSF pressure within minutes (> 85-95% immediate success rate).

options.text: Perform a repeat lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position to inject 20 mL of preservative-free normal saline into the intrathecal space
options.explanation: Intrathecal saline injection provides only transient (minutes to hours) pressure restoration and introduces a second dural puncture hole, doubling the CSF leak rate.

options.text: Initiate oral sumatriptan 100 mg twice daily as first-line therapy for acute dural migraine
options.explanation: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists for vascular migraine; multiple randomized trials have shown that triptans are completely ineffective for mechanical low-pressure post-dural puncture headaches.

options.explanation: Superficial temporal artery ligation has no role in low-CSF-pressure orthostatic headaches and represents an inappropriate, mutilating surgical intervention.

subject: Medicine
topic: Hypertensive Emergency vs Hypertensive Urgency Cross-Coverage
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department at 11:00 PM with severe shortness of breath, orthopnea, and chest tightness that began 2 hours ago. He has a history of essential hypertension but has not taken his prescribed amlodipine or hydrochlorothiazide for 3 weeks because he ran out of medication. subject: Surgery
topic: Post-Thyroidectomy Acute Hypocalcemia Management
stem:
A 42-year-old woman who underwent an uncomplicated total thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter 24 hours ago is recovering on the surgical ward. At 4:00 AM, the cross-covering resident is called because the patient has developed tingling and numbness around her mouth (circumoral paresthesias) and painful cramping in both hands. Physical examination reveals an anxious woman. When a blood pressure cuff on her right arm is inflated to 20 mm Hg above her systolic pressure for 3 minutes, her right wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints involuntarily flex with extension of the interphalangeal joints and adduction of the thumb (positive Trousseau sign). Tapping gently over the facial nerve anterior to the ear tragus produces ipsilateral contraction of the facial muscles (positive Chvostek sign). Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 122/76 mm Hg and heart rate of 88/min. A 12-lead ECG reveals sinus rhythm with marked prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc 510 ms). Emergent laboratory evaluation demonstrates:
- Total serum calcium: 6.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.2 mg/dL)
- Serum albumin: 4.0 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL)
- Ionized calcium: 0.82 mmol/L (normal 1.15 to 1.33 mmol/L)
- Serum magnesium: 2.0 mg/dL (normal 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL)
- Serum phosphate: 5.4 mg/dL (elevated; normal 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL)

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate medical management for this patient?

options.text: Administer an immediate intravenous bolus of 10% calcium chloride 10 mL via a small 22-gauge peripheral hand vein
options.explanation: Intravenous calcium chloride is highly caustic and sclerosing; infusing it through a peripheral hand vein carries severe risks of peripheral thrombophlebitis and catastrophic full-thickness skin necrosis if extravasation occurs; calcium gluconate is preferred.

options.text: Administer oral calcium carbonate 500 mg monotherapy once daily and recheck serum calcium in 48 hours
options.explanation: Oral calcium monotherapy is completely inadequate for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia with QTc prolongation and tetany, and without calcitriol, oral calcium absorption is poor in hypoparathyroidism.

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus as primary standalone therapy without calcium
options.explanation: Serum magnesium is normal (2.0 mg/dL); while hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia, giving magnesium when levels are normal does not treat the acute profound calcium deficit.

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate (1 to 2 g in 50 to 100 mL of 5% dextrose infused over 10 to 20 minutes) with continuous cardiac telemetry monitoring, followed by maintenance oral calcium carbonate and oral calcitriol
options.explanation: Acute Hypocalcemia is a well-recognized complication occurring in up to 10% to 30% of patients following total thyroidectomy, caused by transient ischemia, devascularization, surgical trauma, or inadvertent excision of the parathyroid glands during thyroid lobe dissection: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND NEUROMUSCULAR HYPEREXCITABILITY: Extracellular calcium ions stabilize neuronal and muscle cell membranes by blocking sodium channels. In severe hypocalcemia, this stabilizing effect is lost, dramatically lowering the threshold for action potential generation and provoking spontaneous, repetitive firing of peripheral nerves. (2) CLINICAL HALLMARKS: (a) Circumoral and digital paresthesias; (b) Neuromuscular irritability: Chvostek sign (facial twitching upon percussion of CN VII) and Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm induced by cuff inflation; more sensitive and specific than Chvostek); (c) Tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, and ECG QTc prolongation (predisposing to torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia). (3) IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY PHARMACOTHERAPY: (a) INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM GLUCONATE: Symptomatic acute hypocalcemia (ionized Ca < 0.9 mmol/L, tetany, QTc prolongation) is an emergency requiring IMMEDIATE INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM GLUCONATE (1-2 g of 10% calcium gluconate [equivalent to 90-180 mg elemental calcium] infused over 10-20 minutes). CALCIUM GLUCONATE IS PREFERRED OVER CALCIUM CHLORIDE because calcium chloride causes severe tissue necrosis and thrombophlebitis if extravasation occurs; calcium chloride is reserved for cardiac arrest via central lines. (b) ORAL CONSOLIDATION: Once acute tetany is relieved, initiate high-dose oral calcium (calcium carbonate 1,000-2,000 mg three times daily) COMBINED WITH ORAL CALCITRIOL (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, 0.25-0.5 mcg twice daily), which is essential to stimulate active intestinal calcium absorption in the presence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism.

options.text: Return the patient emergently to the operating room for surgical exploration of the neck incision
options.explanation: The patient has hypocalcemic tetany from transient parathyroid stunning, not a compressive postoperative neck hematoma (wound is non-tense, breathing is uncompromised); re-operation is unnecessary and harmful.

subject: Medicine
topic: Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury (CA-AKI) Prevention
stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, estimated GFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2) is scheduled to undergo an elective contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) angiography of the chest and abdomen to evaluate a suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm. He has no history of heart failure and takes metformin (which was withheld 24 hours ago) and amlodipine. Physical examination reveals normal blood pressure (130/78 mm Hg), normal jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, and no peripheral edema. The medical resident inquires about the optimal pharmacological strategy to prevent contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI).

Based on landmark randomized clinical trial evidence (the PRESERVE trial) and current KDIGO/ACR guidelines, which of the following represents the most appropriate, evidence-based preventive strategy for this high-risk patient?

options.text: Administer oral N-acetylcysteine 1,200 mg twice daily for 48 hours combined with intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion
options.explanation: The landmark PRESERVE trial (> 5,000 patients) proved that neither N-acetylcysteine nor sodium bicarbonate reduces contrast-induced AKI or mortality compared to isotonic saline; their routine use is contrary to guidelines.

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg 1 hour prior to contrast injection to ensure high tubular flow rates
options.explanation: Forced diuresis with furosemide causes intravascular volume depletion, worsening renal medullary vasoconstriction and significantly INCREASING the incidence of contrast nephropathy.

options.text: Administer prophylactic oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily as an adenosine receptor antagonist
options.explanation: Theophylline has narrow therapeutic margins, significant cardiac arrhythmogenic toxicity, and lacks consistent clinical trial support; it is not recommended by KDIGO.

options.text: Perform prophylactic hemodialysis immediately following completion of the CT angiogram
options.explanation: Prophylactic hemodialysis removes contrast but causes transient hemodynamic instability that worsens renal ischemia, and clinical trials prove it provides zero benefit while increasing complications.

options.text: Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (0.9% normal saline at 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/hour for 3 to 12 hours prior to and 6 to 12 hours following contrast administration), while withholding oral N-acetylcysteine and intravenous sodium bicarbonate
options.explanation: Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury (CA-AKI; historically contrast-induced nephropathy) is defined as an abrupt decline in renal function occurring within 48 hours of intravascular iodinated radiocontrast administration. (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Iodinated contrast triggers intense renal medullary vasoconstriction (endothelin and adenosine release with decreased nitric oxide), causing profound ischemic injury to metabolically active thick ascending limbs and proximal tubules, compounded by direct tubular epithelial cell cytotoxicity and reactive oxygen species generation. (2) EVIDENCE-BASED INTRAVENOUS EXPANSION: Intravenous volume expansion with ISOTONIC CRYSTALLOIDS (0.9% normal saline or lactated Ringer solution) is the ONLY intervention proven to consistently reduce CA-AKI. Hydration expands intravascular volume, suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, dilutes contrast medium in the tubular lumen, promotes tubular contrast transit, and prevents medullary vasoconstriction. (3) THE LANDMARK PRESERVE TRIAL (NEJM 2018): For years, oral N-acetylcysteine (an antioxidant) and intravenous sodium bicarbonate (to alkalinize tubular urine) were widely utilized based on small, flawed historical studies. The landmark double-blind randomized PRESERVE trial (involving > 5,000 high-risk patients with CKD undergoing angiography) definitively tested sodium bicarbonate vs sodium chloride, and oral N-acetylcysteine vs placebo. The trial proved that NEITHER SODIUM BICARBONATE NOR N-ACETYL CYSTEINE REDUCED THE INCIDENCE OF AKI, THE NEED FOR DIALYSIS, OR 90-DAY MORTALITY compared to standard isotonic normal saline and placebo. Current KDIGO and American College of Radiology (ACR) guidelines explicitly recommend AGAINST routine N-acetylcysteine or routine sodium bicarbonate, establishing ISOTONIC SALINE AS THE PRIMARY EVIDENCE-BASED PROPHYLAXIS.
